column1: # Where each gloss in lex-es.tsv was read.
# lemma | pos | tgt | sources | quote | stands
# The gloss is the English word a Spanish word is woven for, and the tooltip
# prints it back: it is the claim every reader meets first. Every other claim
# the pack makes about a word names its entry — genders in es-genders.tsv,
# plurals in es-plurals.tsv, verb forms in es-verb-forms.tsv — and the gloss
# named none until 2026-10-08, the night fr-glosses.tsv was written the same
# Every row is read, all 356: the 178 nouns, 81 verbs, 57 adjectives, 22
# adverbs, 13 numerals and 5 interjections. Each was read in the rendered
# page of the word's English Wiktionary entry, in its Spanish section: a
# script took the definition lines under each heading of the row's part of
# speech, examples, quotations and synonyms set aside, and drafted the first
# that holds the row's English word, and every quote was read against its
# page. Where that first line is another sense, the quote is the row's: ley's
# first is "law (a well-established characteristic of nature)", and its line
# quotes "law (body of rules issued by a legislative body)"; pelo's first is
# "hair (a single hair)", and its line quotes the hair of a head, the sense
# muy's one line begins with Wiktionary's own notice, "(Can we verify this
# sense?)", which asks whether it is an apocopic form of mucho; its quote
# leaves the notice out and keeps the rest of the line, "very" among it.
# A page holds every word of one spelling, so a quote is from this word's
# own part of speech where the page has it. Four rows' words have none of
# theirs, and their lines quote the heading the page gives them: solo, woven
# for "alone" among the adverbs, is "alone, by oneself" as an adjective, its
# adverb being "only; solely; just"; cien, "hundred", is a "Number"; primero,
# "first", an ordinal adjective; and sí, "yes", a particle, its page's
# interjection being "(Spain) hello?", the answer to a telephone.
# The title is the word as Wiktionary's address writes it: without a
# homograph's number, and with an underscore for a space, so that each source
# stays one word of the field: wikt:es:estar_de_pie. A noun cites the entry
# its gender was read in, which for every Spanish noun is its own.
# Three pages define nothing and name another form, so their lines quote the
# entry named and cite the word's own beside it, as the Old English ledger
# does, the quoted entry first: sentarse is "infinitive of sentar combined
# with se", and its line quotes sentar's "(pronominal) to sit down, have a
# seat"; juntos is "masculine plural of junto", and its line quotes junto's
# adverb, "together"; and quizás is "alternative form of quizá", "perhaps,
# maybe". FORM_OF in tests/tools/glosses.test.ts lists them.
# One phrase has no entry at all. English Wiktionary has none for en ningún
# lugar, "nowhere", nor for en ninguna parte, en ningún lado or en ningún
# sitio. It is its words, en, "in", ningún, "not any", and lugar, "place", so
# its line cites the three entries and quotes a line of each, joined by
# " / ", and names no stand-in, no one word of it meaning "nowhere".
# COMPOSED in the test lists it with its words.
# Blank where the quote holds the row's English word. Otherwise it names the
# word of the quote that stands for it, because the English word is not in
# the entry. Five rows need one: extraño for "stranger" is "foreigner",
# barco for "ship" "boat (usually with a concave hull)", abrigo for "coat"
# "overcoat", subir for "rise" "to go up or come up", and verdaderamente for
# None is false. Two say less than the row is woven for, and are recorded
# rather than changed: extraño's noun is only "foreigner", where a stranger
# need not be foreign — the adjective is "strange, unusual" and "foreign,
# alien" — and verdaderamente's only line is "truthfully", where English
# tests/tools/glosses.test.ts requires every row of lex-es.tsv to have a line
# here citing its own word's entry, whose quote holds its English word or the
# stand-in it names, and fails on a line outliving its row.

column5: person (an individual; usually a human being)
family (group of people related to each other)
mister, sir, lord (title conferred on a married or older male)
neighbour (a person living on adjacent or nearby land)
(anatomy) outer ear; auricle; ear (used for references to the external or tangible aspects of the ear)
nose (a protuberance on the face housing the nostrils, which are used to breathe or smell)
(anatomy) digit: finger or toe, literally translated as "finger" and thought of that way by Spanish-speaking learners of English
(anatomy) face (the front part of the head)
body (the physical structure of a human or animal)
dog (the species Canis familiaris (sometimes designated Canis lupus familiaris), domesticated for thousands of years and of highly variable appearance because of human breeding)
fish (especially if alive or not intended for consumption)
cow (adult female of the species Bos taurus)
snake, serpent (legless reptile of the sub-order Serpentes)
bread (food made by baking cereal dough)
wine (an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grape juice, with an ABV ranging from 5.5–16%)
an animal’s meat, or by extension the edible “fleshy” or soft part of a fruit or vegetable
fruit (the seed-bearing part of a plant)
door (portal of entry into a building)
wall, especially of a house or room
bridge (construction spanning a waterway, ravine, or valley from an elevated height)
(countable) sword (a long bladed weapon with a grip and typically a pommel and crossguard (together forming a hilt), which is designed to cut, stab, slash and/or hack)
stone (hard earthen substance that can form large rocks)
(clothing) cloth, fabric (woven material made of fibers)
Earth (planet of the Solar System in which all of humanity resides)
(geography) land, ground (Earth surface not covered by oceans or other bodies of water)
leaf (usually green and flat organ that is the most prominent feature of most vegetative plants)
(chiefly Spain, uncountable) grass (plant of the family Poaceae or plant that resembles grasses)
trail, path, track (a route for travel over land)
shadow (a dark image projected onto a surface where light (or other radiation) is blocked by the shade of an object)
night (the period between sunset and sunrise)
hour (a time period of sixty minutes)
law (body of rules issued by a legislative body)
story (a sequence of real or fictional events)
(with ser or (chiefly Latin America, sometimes) estar) good (of good quality)
(with ser or (chiefly Latin America, sometimes) estar) bad (of bad quality)
(after the noun or predicatively) big, large
long (having much distance from one terminating point to another)
short (having a small distance from one end to another)
low, ground (situated close to the ground)
(of an object) old (having existed for a long time)
rich (having a lot of money and possessions)
sad, saddened, blue, gloomy, unhappy, joyless, triste
difficult, hard, tough, challenging, rough, tricky, trying, arduous, testing
deep (having a bottom far from the surface or mouth)
black (absorbing all light and reflecting none; dark and hueless)
to say, to tell, to name, to mention
(intransitive) to go (away from speaker and listener)
(sometimes reflexive) to come (move closer to some location (most often closer to the speaker), by default the speaker's location)
(chiefly Latin America unless imperative) to take (put under one's physical or mental control, often in one's hands)
to desire, to want, to want to

to talk; to speak; to communicate using words [with con ‘with’, along with de or sobre ‘about’, along with en ‘in (a language)’, along with dative ‘person spoken to’, along with accusative ‘what is said’]
(intransitive or transitive) to write (to form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate)
(pronominal) to sit down, have a seat
(idiomatic) to stand (to be upright, support oneself on the feet in an erect position)
(intransitive, sometimes reflexive) to die (to stop living)
(somewhat literary) to love, have great affection for, care about
to hold, to hold up, to prop up, to sustain, to underpin (physically)
to bring (in the sense of transport, for differences with llevar and examples see that entry)
to buy (to obtain in exchange of money or goods)
(transitive) to pay [with le ‘someone’; or with lo ‘something or someone’]
(transitive, intransitive, reflexive) to open, open up
to start, begin, to get started
(transitive, intransitive) to learn (to acquire, or attempt to acquire knowledge or an ability to do something)
to fight, to battle, to do battle
(transitive, often reflexive) to laugh [with de ‘at, about’]
(intransitive or transitive) to wait, wait (for) [(optionally) with direct object ‘for something’ or a que (+ subjunctive clause) ‘for something to happen’]
(transitive) to watch (to look at, view, or observe for a period of time)
(transitive) to look at (to try to see, to pay attention to with one’s eyes)
(transitive or ditransitive) to put, to place (cause to assume a specified position)
to go out, to leave, to depart, to head out
to seek, search for, look for, try to find, to scour
(transitive, intransitive) to change, to shift, to switch, to alter
(intransitive, reflexive) to fall (to move to a lower position due to gravity)
to go up or come up
(transitive) to move (to cause to change place or posture)
(idiomatic) everywhere, all over the place, all around, throughout
in, at, on / (before the noun) apocopic form of ninguno (“not any”) / place
(before adjectives and adverbs) apocopic form of mucho; very
yes, yeah, (used to respond affirmatively to a question, used both informally and formally)
